- The Boat investigation has begun from `https://boat.dev/`; its homepage and the 107-line documentation index at `https://docs.boat.dev/llms.txt` were fetched successfully, but the linked documentation review and comparison with existing sandbox research remain incomplete.
- A web search describes boat.dev as ASCII's sandbox platform, previously launched as box, providing persistent Ubuntu VMs with Docker, SSH, browser or desktop access, snapshots, and forking for agent workloads; Anicet Nougaret is identified in the search results as an ASCII cofounder associated with its launch. These identity and product-history details remain secondary-source findings.
- Boat documentation reports no idle timer: auto-stop TTL starts at sandbox creation or resume, numeric TTL is capped at 30 days, and command calls are not retried automatically because a timed-out or failed call may already be running. The documentation also reports full VMs with sudo, SOC 2 in progress, dedicated IPv6 or IPv4 addresses, and egress included up to 2 TB per sandbox per month; the implications for the project's sandbox and egress design remain unreviewed.
- Additional Boat documentation reports EU sandbox regions in Germany, Finland, and France with data and snapshots remaining there, approximately 100–200 ms round trips from the US or Latin America, stopped sandboxes being free with snapshots retained for the sandbox lifetime, full VMs with passwordless `sudo` and `systemd`, Docker with BuildKit, public IPv4 or IPv6, no GPU, and `/dev/kvm` support for QEMU/KVM, Firecracker, and Android emulators. Compliance status remains limited because SOC 2 is in progress; the implications for the project's regionality, virtualization, and trust requirements remain unreviewed.
- Boat documentation reports machine-time pricing of $0.018/hour for `small`, $0.036/hour for `default`, $0.072/hour for `large`, and $0.200/hour for `xlarge`; stopped sandboxes and automatic snapshots are free, while named snapshots beyond the first 10 cost $1.70/month each. The same documentation reports a 4-vCPU/8-GB benchmark of 27.7 runs/second for Boat versus 13.0 for Vercel Sandbox, 11.2 for E2B, and 9.6 for Modal, with measurements taken on different dates and described as indicative rather than like-for-like. The pricing and benchmark comparison remain documentation-reported rather than independently validated in this project.
- Boat documentation reports that an environment can be marked safe for third parties, in which case GitHub access, secrets, sandbox credentials, and agent credentials are not passed into the sandbox and the sandbox is confined to itself; `boat new --no-env` provides the same per-sandbox guarantee. The implications for the project's sandbox trust and credential-isolation design remain unreviewed.
- Boat's homepage describes persistent Ubuntu virtual machines with SSH and SCP, Docker, dedicated IPv6 or IPv4 addresses, a 60fps virtual desktop, snapshot-based disk-level forking, and preinstalled development tools including VS Code, Chrome, Ghostty, the GitHub CLI, Rust, Node.js, and Bun; these product claims remain documentation-reported rather than independently validated in this project.
- Boat documentation reports that a normal sandbox receives account environment variables and credential files, while a protected sandbox retains only neutral Boat-internal variables and explicitly passed values. The documentation reports that `boat resume <id> --no-env` and `boat fork <id> --no-env` scrub owner credentials from snapshots before access, leave credentials created inside the sandbox by other software untouched, return a retryable `boat_securing` error during scrubbing, and make the conversion one-way; the implications for the project's credential-isolation design remain unreviewed.
- Boat documentation reports that each sandbox and its integrated agents share one browser-accessible desktop screen, so concurrent GUI-driving conversations conflict. It also reports that archived filesystem snapshots remain available for resume or fork, named snapshots are independent retained artifacts, and zero-data-retention is unavailable after archive; the implications for parallel computer-use evaluation and data-retention requirements remain unreviewed.
